translations.text: An encomium delivered by the honored patriarch and chief teacher, Apa Celestine, archbishop of the city of Rome.
He delivered it in praise of the martyrs’ pride, the true crown-bearer of Christ, the holy virgin, Saint Victor the general.
He delivered it on the day of his holy commemoration, the twenty-seventh of the month of Pharmouthi.
He delivered it in his martyr shrine, which the God-loving emperor built for him in Rome.
He also spoke about the piercing of the soul, making it clear that nothing in human life is lasting except suffering and misery.

He also spoke about what is written in the Apostle: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of God,” and about a person’s great helplessness at the moment when he gives his spirit into God’s hands.
He delivered this encomium while Emperor Valentinian was sitting beside him, together with the entire senate and all the people, men and women.
They were celebrating the feast of the general, Saint Victor, and, indeed, marveling at the wisdom of Saint Celestine. In the peace of God.
May his holy blessings come down upon us, and may we all be saved together. Amen. Bless us.
Whenever the Creator himself, the savior of his own creation and the sustainer who is full of every compassion, is pleased in his mercy
to remember the work of his hands, to give them their food in its season, to open his hand, which is full of all righteousness, and to make the sky pour down rainwater at the proper time,
then the fields become green and sprout, and all humanity rejoices.
The moistening of the earth with rainwater in its season.
The farmer breaks up the clod of the field with the plow, and they cast seed into it at sowing time, and it begins to sprout seeds for sowing of every kind.
And everyone experiences great delight,
as they enjoy their food and bodily sustenance, extending even to the animals of the field.
They leap and bound as they eat the grass of the sowing season.
And the farmers rejoice greatly, confident that they can pay their taxes from their fields.
If such joy comes about because of bodily food, how much greater, then, is today’s joy, O flock of rational sheep
and blessed people of the Christians! For the blood that came from God’s side, together with the water, fell upon the earth.
It renewed the world once again and became a spring of water gushing up to eternal life.
All humanity rejoiced, and they all leaped for joy.
They sprouted again through the water and the blood that came from the side of Emmanuel.
They brought forth spiritual fruits, which are the virtues of the Holy Spirit.
Some chose purity for themselves from their birth until their end.
Others have wives but live as though they had none.
Some practice self-discipline from their youth to their old age, with rigorous fasting.
Some renounced the world.
They went to the mountains.
They became monks, pursuing the good struggle until the day of their death.
Others took up their crosses and followed the Lord.
They shed their blood for their confession of God and received the crown of martyrdom.
In short, all humanity blossomed and bore fruit with great joy.
The written word was fulfilled in this generation: “They will all know you, from the least to the greatest.”
For our Savior is among us today with his angels, celebrating the feast of the general, Apa Victor, on the day of his commemoration, which is today.
All the heavenly ranks are gathered with us today.
They honor the one who renounced the world and its riches and received the perfect kingdom.
The prophets and martyrs are among us today, celebrating the feast of the one who renounced the world and its riches.
Christ loved him and crowned him with the crown of the kingdom of heaven.
O general, Saint Victor!
O crowned one among the martyrs!
O invincible master of the contest!
O true crown-bearer of Christ!
O you who made your body a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God!
I want to speak praises of you at your feast today, but I am afraid that I cannot cross the ocean of your achievements.
For my tongue is a tongue of flesh, and the heart within me is a human heart. I cannot tell of your glory and the honor with which God has adorned you.
Who among all the wise people of the world could ever fully describe your honor, O Saint Victor?
For you have been a virgin since your youth.
You are a remarkable ascetic.
You fast two days at a time throughout your life.
The door of your house is open to everyone.
For this reason I am afraid to set out upon the ocean of your virtues.
I know the weakness of my tongue and of my heart, which has no wisdom in it.
In what way shall I honor you and [?]?
You are a virgin like Elijah, and you have never had intercourse with a woman.
You are a good, righteous man, considerate toward all the poor, like Abraham the patriarch.
You are a mighty martyr among all the martyrs.
You were not afraid of kings, military commanders, or governors, nor could the tortures change your resolve.

The threats of your father Romanus could not make you stumble in your loyalty to your true father, Christ. Instead, you remained firmly established upon the unshakable rock, Christ, until your last breath.
O righteous man in his generation, who made his body a sacrifice to God!
What shall I say, or what shall I declare about you, O Saint Victor?
If I compare you to Noah, you have become perfect like him in our generation.
If I compare you to Abraham, you are hospitable like him, for God visited Abraham with his angels because of his hospitality.
To you too, O Saint Victor, Christ, the Son of God, came in the form of a poor man.
He comforted you in the fortress in a desert land because of the great sufferings you endured for his holy name.
If I compare you to Isaac the patriarch, his parents took him against his will to offer him up as a sacrifice to the Lord.
But you, O Saint Victor, of your own free choice,
offered up your body as a whole burnt offering to the Lord through the many tortures you endured for the name of Christ.
If I compare you to Jacob the patriarch, Christ took his name from him.
But as for you, O Saint Victor, all the martyrs in heaven, and also those on earth, have boasted of you because of your endurance.
If I compare you to Joseph, you fought against the passions as he did.
Joseph was handed over into slavery by his brothers.
But as for you, O Saint Victor, it was your father who handed you over because of the name of Christ.
Joseph attained kingship because of his endurance.
But you, O Saint Victor, attained the kingdom of heaven.
If I compare you to Melchizedek and Aaron, they offered up sheep and calves as symbolic sacrifices.
But you, Saint Victor, made your own body an offering to God.
For this reason, you received great glory in the kingdom of heaven.
If I compare you to Moses the lawgiver, you too renounced military command in this world, your parents’ wealth, and your possessions.
You took up your cross and followed your Lord.
Moses refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. Instead, he chose to suffer with God’s people rather than enjoy sin for a time.
You too, Saint Victor, refused to be called the son of Romanus, the first to be greeted by the emperor.
You renounced the rank of military commander and your wealth.
You followed the one who said, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.”
You received the military command that lasts forever.
If I compare you to Isaiah the prophet, you too beheld the one who sits upon the cherubim and seraphim.
He came to you and rescued you from all your afflictions.
And he honored you in heaven and on earth.
In heaven, he made you a commander among all the martyrs, as we will explain to you as our account proceeds.
On earth too, he honored you, so that your sweet fragrance filled all the lands of the world.
And shrines are built for you everywhere, and great miracles and wonders take place through them,
to the glory of God and his holy martyr.
For the written saying is true: “Whoever gives me glory, my Father will honor him.”
For throughout your life you took no part in the cares of this world, but all your devotion was directed toward the love of God.
For this reason, God bestowed this great gift on you: he placed in your sanctuary a power that heals souls and bodies.
For you heal bodily illnesses through the grace God has given you. As for illnesses of the soul, which are sins,
you cleanse them through the signs and wonders you reveal in your shrine in the four corners of the world.
Saint Victor, your blood that was poured out brought down the pillar of Baal, as Elijah did, and you destroyed the idols and their pillars.
You became a pillar for the whole company of martyrs.
You quenched the fiery flame through the power of God that was with you, like the three holy men.
To whom in Scripture, then, shall I compare you and find that you are not his equal—not to say that you surpass him?
What shall I say about you, O healer of hidden and visible diseases?
Indeed, he even raised the dead with oil from the lamp of his martyr’s shrine, where you are gathered today. And I saw the miracle with my own eyes.
I am the least of all.
But let no one disbelieve the miracle that happened, lest the written saying be fulfilled concerning him: “The unbeliever does not have a single penny.”
Listen now, and I will explain the matter to you, to the glory of God and Saint Victor, whose feast we are celebrating today.
For indeed our Savior said, “Whoever believes in me—the works that I do in my Father’s name,
he too will do them, and he will do greater things than these.”
Now there was a man in this city whose name was Alexander.
He was extremely rich in gold and silver.
He had a wife who was barren.
She had never borne a child, and there was great sorrow in their hearts over this, because they had no heir to their estate.
They heard about the mighty deeds and miracles taking place through the shrine of Saint Apa Victor.
They got up together and went to the holy place.
They brought their gifts into the shrine on Sunday.
Afterward they made a vow, saying, “Hear us today as we implore you.
If your mercy reaches us and you give us offspring, we will dedicate him to your shrine until the day of his death.
Only take away our disgrace and grant us our request.”
When they had said these things, they went home joyfully.
Then one day Saint Victor interceded with Christ on their behalf.
The woman bore a son who was very beautiful to look at, and God’s grace surrounded him.
They named him Victor, after Saint Victor.
There was great joy in their house, and they distributed abundant alms to the poor.
But when the little boy was five years old, his parents could not bring themselves to give him to the sanctuary of Saint Apa Victor,
in accordance with what had come from their mouths. Instead, they went back on their vow.
They did not remember what is written: “Take care to do what comes from your mouth, for the Lord will thoroughly examine your ways and exact punishment from you.”
Then the little boy’s father and mother spoke to each other, saying, “Look, we have not been able to bring ourselves to give the little boy to the sanctuary as we vowed.
Let us call a man in the city who buys slaves, and let him appraise the little boy. Then we will give his price to the sanctuary, so that the martyr will not be angry with us.”
Then they got up and called a merchant in the city who was buying slaves and selling all his goods.
He set the little boy’s price at forty gold coins, and they took the gold.
They brought it into the martyr’s shrine.
They did not remember what is written: “If you make a vow to the Lord your God, you must fulfill it.”
But when Saint Victor saw that the little boy’s parents had not fulfilled their vow honestly,
but instead thought that God’s gift could be obtained with money,
he caused something like this to happen, so that they would be punished for their foolishness.
One day, the little boy was in the street, enjoying himself with children his own age near his parents’ house.
Suddenly, a large stone from the corner of the house fell on the little boy.
He fell down and died immediately.
When his parents heard, they tore their clothes and screamed loudly.
They came outside with the slaves.
They found the little boy dead.
Oh, how great was the sorrow at that moment!
They cried out, “Woe to us, beloved son!
We are the ones responsible for your death, because we made a vow but did not fulfill our vow to give you to the saint’s shrine.
Look, he has taken you from us before we had enjoyed enough time with you.
He has set our hearts burning with grief for our beloved son.
We are the ones who deserve death.
We do not know what we will do from this moment on.”
But his father took courage with firm faith.
He took his little son in his arms, while the boy’s mother and his slaves followed him.
They brought him into Saint Victor’s martyr shrine.
He laid him down before the altar.
He cried out, saying, “Saint Victor, I know that you have power to do anything, and you are the one who graciously gave me this little boy.
Do not treat me according to my foolishness, but have compassion on my tears and return the little boy’s soul to him once again.”
And we, together with him, will serve you until the day of our death.
After saying these things while weeping, he took a little oil from the lamp.
He marked the little boy with the sign of the cross using it, and applied it to his mouth, his nose, and his heart.
The miracle that happened at that moment surpassed that of Elijah and Elisha.
For as soon as the oil from the lamp touched the little boy, the one who said, “I strike, and my hand heals,”
restored the little boy’s soul once again. And through the prayers of Saint Victor, he opened his eyes.
Great was the joy that came upon his parents that day, and upon everyone belonging to their household.
They cried out in a loud voice, “You are great, O God of Saint Victor, and there is no other besides you in heaven or on earth!
Instead of sorrow, you have given us gladness.
You have raised the little boy for his parents after he had died.”
When the crowd saw the great miracle that had happened, they cried out in a loud voice.
They ran toward the little boy.
They cried out, saying, “The God of Saint Victor is the one God!”
The little boy’s father went around the whole city with him, holding his hand and proclaiming the miracles of Saint Victor.
Afterward, he went to his house.
He brought all his possessions and his slaves.
He gave them to the sanctuary of Saint Victor.
He continued serving him until the day of his death. And the little boy became an outstanding man, remaining a virgin throughout his life.
Afterward, he attained the rank of priest. And it was said about him that he saw Saint Victor many times, as he appeared to him.
For the saying that our Savior spoke is indeed true: “My Father will honor whoever serves me.”
You see, my beloved, how powerful the prayer of Saint Victor is.
And whoever makes a vow and does not fulfill his vow, God punishes him.
We too, if we make a vow to the martyrs,
let us fulfill it diligently, so that they will not be angry with us.
For it is a great sin to make a vow and then regret what you have vowed.
But so that we do not linger over the account,
let us return and tell you another great miracle that happened at the shrine of Saint Victor, to the glory of God and his holy martyrs.
There was a woman in this city named Callieutropia. She was the daughter of Emperor Honorius’s sister.
She was extremely wealthy.
One day, during the summer, she was sleeping at noon in a cave in her house.
A demon plunged into her two breasts.
They swelled and became terribly distended.
They grew hard, becoming as hard as stone as they hung from her.
She was weeping [?] and was in great torment day and night.
She spent large sums on doctors.
She obtained no cure, but continued to suffer torment.
Her family gave up on her.
The doctors in particular made every effort, but they could not cure her, even though she was the emperor’s sister.
Instead, they were powerless against the suffering caused by the disease, just as it is written about them: “Their wisdom failed them.”
When she heard about the mighty deeds and miracles taking place at the shrine of Saint Victor, she begged her husband and her brother
to let her go to the saint’s shrine, so that perhaps his mercy might reach her and he might grant her healing.
Her family agreed to her request.
They could see that she was in danger of dying.
They ordered that she be placed in a litter and taken to the shrine of Saint Victor.
When she entered the shrine, she cried out, “My lord, Saint Victor, I beg you, have mercy on me and take this suffering away from me, for you are a saint of God.”
At midnight, Saint Victor took pity on the woman’s plight.
He brought her relief.
She fell asleep, with her servants and eunuchs gathered around her.
He came to her in a vision, wearing a purple robe and radiating rays of light, with a staff of light in his hand.
He said to her, “If you want to get well,
When you get up early tomorrow, take a little oil from the lamp burning in front of the altar and anoint your breasts.
The demon will be shaken and come out, and you will be free of this suffering.
But guard yourself against harshness toward your slaves, and be careful not to go about with this arrogant bearing again. Reach out your hand to the poor.
For this suffering overtook you because of your mercilessness and your pride.
The woman became deeply troubled.
She answered fearfully, “Who are you, surrounded by all this great glory?”
He answered in a gentle voice, “I am Victor, the commander of the great King.”
When he had said this, she could no longer see him.
Immediately she awoke from the vision.
She smelled a strong, sweet fragrance that had filled the entire martyr’s shrine, and she said to herself, “Truly, it was Saint Victor who was speaking with me—
me, a sinner.”
Immediately she woke her attendants.
She told them about the vision.
When morning came, she went to the priest of the martyr’s shrine.
He gave her a little oil from the lamp.
When he handed it to her, she anointed her breasts, saying, “In the name of the God of Saint Victor, whose glory I was found worthy to see, grant me healing.”
Immediately the demon was shaken.
It sprang out of her breasts like a vulture, while the people watched it looking like a flame of fire. Immediately her breasts returned to their former condition.
She cried out, “The God of Saint Victor is one!”
She gave valuable gifts to the martyr’s shrine—a great deal of gold and silver—as a memorial of the healing she had received.
Afterward she went home to her people, glorifying God and his holy martyr.
We must also tell you about another great miracle that took place through this saint.
When Emperor Honorius saw the healing his sister had received through Saint Victor, he rejoiced greatly.
He decided to reinforce the apse of the altar and the woodwork of the martyr’s shrine with pure gold, as a memorial honoring the saint.
He had craftsmen brought who were masters of their craft.
They worked on the altar to fashion it out of gold.
While they were still working on the wooden framework, the devil, the hater of what is good, knocked down one of the craftsmen who were working.
He fell down.
The other craftsmen were frightened.
They cried out, “Lord, have mercy!” And the king and the other people below were alarmed at what had happened.
At that very moment, Saint Victor came down from heaven, clothed in great glory.
He caught the craftsman by the hand when he was still three cubits above the ground.
He lifted him up and took him to the wooden framework.
He set him on his feet beside the large beam, next to his fellow craftsman.
No harm had come to him, and no one had seen Saint Victor except the craftsman.
When the king and the crowd saw the great miracle that had happened, they were afraid and cried out, “The God of Saint Victor is the one God, and there is no other besides him in heaven or on earth!”
When the craftsman recovered from the fear that had seized him, he reported to the king and all the people, saying, “I saw a huge Ethiopian,
with his wings spread out,
and his eyes blazing like fire.
He thrust in what was in his hands and threw me down.
While I was still falling, there appeared a man of light wearing royal clothing, with his face shining like the sun.
He caught my hand before I reached the ground.
He took me with him and brought me up here.
He placed his seal on me and took away my fear, saying, ‘Do not be afraid. I am Victor, whose martyr’s shrine you are working on.’
And immediately I could no longer see him.”
When the crowd heard these things, they cried out, “The God of Saint Victor is the one God!”
And so, through the diligence of the God-loving king and the miracles of Saint Victor,
they completed the wooden framework and the altar with pure gold and precious stones of great value.
You have seen, my beloved, how great are the miracles of Saint Victor, whose festival we celebrate today.
And everyone who appeals to him with all their heart, even if they are suffering from any illness, he grants them healing.
There was also a man in this city who was a patrician in the service of the emperors. He fell ill with an incurable disease.
His whole body swelled up until it was as thick as a pillar.
It was heartbreaking to see him in this miserable condition.
He was in distress and in great, unbearable pain, so that you would often find him sitting down,
with his servants wrapping him up. His feet and limbs would split open and discharge large amounts of foul matter.
He paid large sums of money to the doctors,
but he found no relief.
Indeed, the emperors of Rome sent chief physicians because he was an important man in the palace. These others also made every effort, but he gained no benefit.
While he was suffering this great pain, he heard about the miracles and wonders taking place at the sanctuary of Saint Apa Victor.
His servants lifted him up and brought him to the saint’s sanctuary.
They laid him in front of the altar.
He cried out day and night, saying, “Saint Victor, look upon my misery and suffering, and grant me healing, for I am suffering terribly.
Or let your mercy reach me, and plead with God on my behalf to take me out of this life, for you see my distress.” That night,
he fell asleep for a little while.
Then Saint Victor took pity on his misfortune, because he loved humanity.
He saw him in a vision, clothed in great glory,
wearing a beautiful purple robe and a golden belt,
radiating rays of light. He said in the vision, “Why are you sick like this?”
The man said to him, “Look, you see my suffering and distress, for I have come close to death.”
The saint said to him with a cheerful face, “I am the one who will heal you, so that you may know that I have power to do anything through the grace of God that is with me.”
He stretched out the staff that was in his hand
and laid it on the sick man, saying, “Healing has reached you today. But do not go on
sinning, or something worse than this may happen to you.
Do not be hard-hearted toward the poor.”
The man answered in alarm, “Who are you, my lord, appearing like this?
I have never seen anyone like you, whether an emperor or a military commander in the palace.”
He answered, “I am Victor, the general of the King of heaven.”
And when he had said these things to him, he stopped discharging foul pus, which had soaked his bed like water, and his swelling subsided.
He became as though he had never been ill.
He sprang up and stood on his feet.
He shouted, “There is one God, the God of Saint Victor!”
When the crowd gathered at the martyr’s shrine saw the great miracle,
they cried out, “How blessed we are to have been found worthy of this precious pearl in our city! He heals our illnesses and our afflictions.”
And he gave gifts of gold and silver to the sanctuary of Saint Victor, so that they could be distributed to the poor and needy.
He went home glorifying God and attending to the salvation of his soul until the day of his death.
What shall I say about the miracles you have performed, O crowned champion of Christ?
What human tongue will be able to proclaim your blessedness, O mighty general?
Truly, even if I spent all my time examining the miracles you have performed, I would not be able to recount a small part of them.
O confessor and tireless champion, who can comprehend the fullness of your honor and the signs that have occurred at your martyr’s shrine?
For just as no one can measure the honor of this saint and the miracles that continually occur at his sanctuary,
O true crowned champion of Christ, the young boy whose wisdom surpassed that of the orators!
O you who despised the kingdom of this world so that you might receive the better one, the kingdom of heaven!
Great is the glory that God has given you in heaven and on earth.
As I said before, your fragrance has filled all the lands of the world, and your name will be spoken in every land,
from the fortress where you met your end as far as the Cataract. And they will glorify you throughout the whole world, because you are great among the martyrs.
Above all, God has caused signs and wonders to continue at your martyr’s shrines everywhere.
And signs of healing [?] are granted to those who believe in your name, and this same gift continues in your martyr’s shrines from one end of the inhabited world to the other.
If not, listen, and I will tell you.
Now it happened, they say, in the early days when the God-loving emperor Constantine built the shrine of Saint Apa Victor, where we are gathered today, that a high-ranking general fell seriously ill.
For six years his insides tormented him, and he did not bathe. He suffered from the disease that doctors call cancer.
And he had paid each of the doctors more than about a hundred pounds of gold.
No relief came to him; instead, he was in danger of dying.
He heard about the mighty deeds and wonders taking place at the shrine of Saint Victor in Antioch.
He got up and went to Antioch.
He spent two days in that shrine without receiving healing.
On the night of the third day, a little rest came upon him through the invincible power of God.
Immediately Saint Victor came to him in a vision,
looking like a mighty military commander,
with his face sending out rays of light.
He said to him, “If you want to be freed from this illness, get up quickly and go to the shrine in Rome.
Then [?] water from the basin at the altar, and you will receive healing.
Was the shrine in Rome worn out, that you came here? Do you not know that my power is throughout the whole world?
The same gift remains in them all for those who believe without doubting. Do you not know that the same power remains in my shrines,
in Rome and Antioch? Why have you brought this hardship upon yourself?
You crossed the open sea and came here.
Do you not know that I have the power to heal here?
But I will not do this here. You must go to my shrine in Rome and receive healing, so that everyone may know my power.”
The man answered, trembling, “My lord, who are you, with this great glory surrounding you?”
He answered, “I am Victor, the military commander.
I will heal your body and give salvation to your soul.”
Immediately he awoke from the vision, trembling greatly.
He said, “Truly, it was Saint Victor who came to visit me.”
Immediately he took courage and said, “Forgive me, my lord Saint Victor, because I neglected to go to your sanctuary, which was newly built in my city, and came here instead.”
At daybreak he woke his servants and the people who had come with him.
He told them about the vision he had seen.
And so he gave great and precious gifts to the shrine in Antioch.
Afterward, he boarded the ship.
He came to the city of Rome.
He went into the shrine of Saint Victor.
He lay down in great distress.
He pleaded with the God of the holy martyr, saying, “My lord, Saint Victor, who made me worthy to see his glory in his shrine in Antioch,
you commanded me to come to this place.
I believe, my lord, that your power fills the whole world, like the sun that shines over the inhabited earth.
Let your mercy reach me, and grant me healing, for I have suffered greatly.”
After saying this, he fell asleep in the evening.
Afterward, he had a little water brought to him from the basin in the sanctuary.
He drank it as Saint Victor had told him, and immediately the God of Saint Victor brought him relief.
He slept soundly throughout the night, contrary to his usual habit.
At daybreak, the martyr came to him in great glory.
He said to him with a face
that was cheerful, “Do you recognize me?”
He said to him, “Yes, my lord, I recognize you: you are Saint Victor.
You are the one who appeared to me in your shrine in Antioch.
You sent me here.”
The saint said to him, “Did I not tell you before that my power fills every place, and that this same power remains in all my shrines, from one end of the earth to the other,
healing everyone who believes without doubting?
Have you not heard what is written: ‘Everything is possible for the one who believes’?”
The man answered, “I believe, my lord, that your power fills every place. But I heard about the miracles taking place in your shrine in Antioch,
and I came seeking healing for my body.”
The saint said to him, “My shrine in Rome is just like my shrine in Antioch.
And in all the churches on earth that have been built in my name, from one end of the earth to the other, my power is at work in them and among those who believe, until the end of this age,
as I heal hidden illnesses and visible ones through the grace that God has given me and all the saints.”
But now, look: I have granted you healing. So now pay attention to the salvation of your soul, so that something worse than this does not happen to you.
When the holy Father Victor had said these things to the man, he hid himself from him.
He woke up in the morning.
He found that his illness had burst inside him; it was the disease called [?].
He discharged a large amount of pus through his mouth.
Immediately he became as though he had never been ill at all.
And he spread the news throughout the whole city of what Saint Victor had said to him.
And from that day onward, whenever anyone suffering from illness, from any illness, went to the holy man's shrine, he granted them healing.
The man gave great gifts to Saint Victor's shrine.
He went home glorifying God, and he kept asking Saint Victor to help him in all his troubles, fasting and praying until the day of his death.
Have you seen, my beloved, how powerful the miracles of this holy man are, whose feast we celebrate today?
And how these mighty works are performed in all his martyr shrines for those who will believe?
Let us too believe with all our heart in the mighty works and miracles of this holy man, so that he may intercede for us before God.
For whoever disbelieves in the mighty works of the saints will not merely receive no benefit; it will also bring condemnation upon him. But now, so that we do not prolong the account,
let us return and tell you about this other great miracle that happened at the shrine of the holy Father Victor, to the glory of God and his saints.
There was a man in this city whose name was Anastasius.
He was very rich and respected for his ancestry.
After he had grown old and reached [?] years of age,
he contracted the disease that physicians call elephantiasis.
His whole body shriveled, and he became leprous and white as snow, so that he was often ashamed before the people who saw him, because his body had become spotted like a leopard.
He was deeply distressed about this, because he was ashamed to go to the palace or to appear in the marketplace because of what had happened to him.
After this, God put it into his heart to go to the martyr shrine of the holy Father Victor and beg him to heal him of his illness by all means.
For he used to see people suffering from various illnesses,
and whenever they went to his martyr shrine, they obtained healing and went home glorifying God.
So he got up in faith.
He went to the shrine of Saint Apa Victor with his servants and large offerings.
He spent two days in the holy place, pleading with Saint Victor to show him mercy and heal him of his leprosy.
He kept saying, “Saint Victor, I believe with all my heart that you have the power to heal me of this leprosy.
Help me, because I am ashamed for people to see me because of what has happened to me.”
After he had spent two days in the martyr’s shrine, a man arrived with inflammation in his eyes. Because of the severity of his suffering, white opacities had developed in his eyes.
He had lost the ability to see with his own eyes.
He had spent everything he owned on doctors.
But no cure had come to him.
Finally, when he heard about Saint Victor’s miracles, he had people take him to the saint’s shrine, suffering great pain.
They laid him on a bed beside the man with leprosy.
He pleaded with the God of Saint Victor, saying, “My lord, the commander, have mercy on me and grant me the light of my eyes.”
We cannot remain silent about the miracle that happened at that time.
That night, God listened to everyone who called out to him sincerely, and he was pleased to heal both men together.
This was through the intercessions of Saint Victor, who performs these wonders and miracles.
That night, after the man with leprosy had eaten with his servants and they had fallen into a deep sleep, Saint Victor took pity on the suffering of the man with leprosy and the blind man.
He wished to reveal his wonders.
He came to the man with leprosy during the night, clothed in great glory, with his face shining very brightly.
He said to him, “Do you recognize who I am?”
He answered, “No, my lord.”
The saint said to him, “I am Victor, the one you plead with every day.
I am the father of this martyr’s shrine.
Now, if you want to be cleansed of your leprosy, when you get up in the morning, take the hand of this blind man sleeping beside you.
Lead him and go down to the pool at the entrance of the martyr’s shrine.
Both of you are to immerse yourselves in it three times, in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.
Then you will see my power: your leprosy will leave you, and the blind man will see.”
Only do not neglect what he told you, and you will be healed.
When Saint Victor had said these things to the leper, he departed from him.
Immediately he awoke from the vision, trembling with fear.
He smelled a strong, sweet fragrance around his sleeping place, like choice incense.
He said to himself, “Truly, it was Saint Victor who came to me to grant me healing.”
He rejoiced greatly and blessed God. Still, he kept the matter in his heart, saying, “I will not tell anyone about the vision,”
as he waited to see how the matter would turn out.
When daylight came, the leper said to the blind man, “Will you get up so that we can go down to the cistern and bathe?
I believe in God and his holy martyr, that he will grant us healing.”
The blind man said to the leper, “Do as you wish.
For look, you see my suffering and my distress.
But I am afraid to bathe, because the doctors instructed me not to put water on my head.”
The leper said to the blind man, “Get up, and let us bathe. God is able to remember us and grant us healing, for we have suffered.”
The blind man agreed to what he said, and the leper took his hand in the midst of the whole crowd.
They went down to the cistern from which the basins of the shrine were filled.
They immersed themselves three times, saying, “In the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the holy martyr, Saint Victor.”
Immediately the leper was healed, and his flesh became like that of a little child.
As for the blind man, the white films in his eyes peeled away.
They fell down into the pool, and his sight was fully restored.
They shouted, saying, “There is one God, the God of Saint Victor, who heals everyone through his holy power!”
When the crowd gathered in the martyr’s shrine heard them, they hurried out to them, looking at the great miracle that had happened.
They cried out, “Great are the mighty works of God and Saint Victor!
Great is the favor God has shown us!
We have been found worthy to have your martyr’s shrine in our city!” Then, when they were told what had happened to them,
the leper revealed everything to them, including how Saint Victor had spoken with him in the vision.
News of this wonder spread everywhere, and I saw it with my own eyes.
I am the least of all, speaking to you in this tribute of praise.
Now the leper and the blind man who had been healed through Saint Victor
remained serving at his martyr shrine until the day of his death, and they received nourishment for the salvation of their souls.
And the pool in which they had bathed became a place of great divine power, which remains there to this very day.
Thus anyone who is sick, whether paralyzed or possessed by a demon—in short, suffering from any illness—
as soon as they bathe in that pool, they receive healing and go home glorifying the God of Saint Victor.
What shall I recount, and what shall I leave out, among your achievements?
Who among all the philosophers in the world could praise you as you deserve?
O you who presented your body as a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable, and pleasing to God!
You endured great sufferings for the name of Christ, O noble Father Victor.
Great is the glory that God has given you in heaven and on earth.
Truly, the written saying has been fulfilled: “The sufferings of the present time are not worthy of the glory that will be revealed to us.”
Great is the honor that God has given you, O holy commander, so that everyone who calls upon God in your name—
whatever distress they may be in—is quickly reached by God's help. And even now,
everyone who implores him with all their heart, he rescues from every danger. If not, listen, and I will tell you.
Now it happened that the barbarians called Saban rose against the land of Romania, as numerous as the sand of the sea,
so that they seized First Romania and prepared many ships to sail across and come against us into Romania.
Now all the people, together with the senate, the entire populace of Rome, and all the nearby surrounding districts,
were gathered, celebrating the common worship service at the sanctuary of Saint Victor, where we are now assembled.
The God-loving emperor was there with the army of soldiers, because it was the feast of Saint Victor. My father Innocent was also there with all the clergy.
When they began the worship service with great awe, letters arrived that had been sent to the emperor
through a courier named Frumentius. The governors of First Romania had sent them to him,
saying, “Quickly prepare the army and reach us without delay to help us, for the barbarians have seized First Armenia!”
The emperor was immediately troubled, as any human would be, but all his hope rested on the Lord.
When he read the letter, he immediately wrote to the governors: “Do not be afraid. I am coming early tomorrow morning with the entire Roman populace.”
When the courier had received the letter and departed,
the king and all the people gathered at the shrine of Saint Victor, together with the archbishop and all the clergy.
They bowed down before the altar, saying, “Saint Victor, commander,
plead with God on our behalf, so that he may defend our country and the godless barbarians may not overpower it.”
In this way they held a great service for the whole congregation, continuing at length until the tenth hour of the day.
Now the miracle that happened at that time must not be passed over.
When they had finished and the archbishop was about to give the people the blessing of peace so that they could return to their homes,
another high-ranking courier arrived, whom the prefect had sent to the king with another letter, bringing great joy. It was written as follows: “Peace to you, God-loving king!
Be victorious and prevail, for God fights on your behalf.
Look, as for the godless barbarians who rose up against your kingdom,
God has struck them down with their own swords.
Each one rose up against the man beside him, beginning at the second hour of the day.
They slaughtered one another. Not one of them survived; they all died.
We have sent all their baggage and their horses to Your Majesty.
So do not trouble yourself or mobilize the military command, for it is God who fights on our behalf together with you.”
Who can oppose us?”
When the king received this letter, he read it aloud to the people before they departed.
They rejoiced exceedingly, with great joy, and immediately understood that it was Saint Victor, the commander, who had struck down the barbarians,
since it was at the second hour of the day that they had appealed to him.
They all cried out loudly, giving glory to God and to Saint Victor. And the barbarians have not invaded the Roman Empire again to this very day.
You have seen, my beloved, how great is the power of the holy commander whose feast we celebrate today.
Let us turn away from every evil deed, every act of violence, every kind of disorder, and every deceit that we practice, so that all of us together may become his children.
Truly, you have made us glad today, Saint Victor, the commander, more than those who make merry in taverns,
for you have set before us the table of your holy feast, filled with every good thing.
Let us, for our part, recognize these things and taste them, so that we may rejoice.
Let us remember the sufferings that our Lord and his servants the martyrs endured for us, and let us bear fruit for God as he deserves, each according to his ability.
One through purity, another through prayer and fasting, one through endurance, another through generosity, and another through love and hospitality.
In short, let none of us remain barren and unfruitful, so that we may become God's cultivated field and sow within ourselves the fruits of righteousness.
Listen to the wise apostle Paul,
who says, “I appeal to you through God's mercies to present your bodies as a living, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God.”
How will we present our bodies, Saint Victor, unless we guard our bodies and our hearts against every deceit and every kind of sexual immorality?
For it is written, “Without purity no one will see God.”
And let us guard our mouths against slander, lying, and speaking any filthy words.
Train your hands, too, for prayer, and keep them from theft and violence.
Let your feet, too, tread the threshold of God's house.
Guard your eyes against lust and against being led into sin by women.
When you observe all these things, you will truly be able to offer your body boldly as a sacrifice to the Lord,
like Saint Victor, who renounced the world and everything in it because of his love for God.
Listen to Peter, the chief apostle,
who says, “I appeal to you, my brothers, as strangers and foreigners, to keep yourselves away from bodily desires, which wage war against your souls.”
So then, my dear friends, we are foreigners on earth.
So then, a person walks about like an image, gathering things without knowing for whom he is gathering them.
If we are strangers and foreigners on earth, then we ought to keep remembering our eternal home, which is the kingdom of God.
We will enter it easily if we keep the commandments entrusted to us.
We were not born to inherit the earth, but for the earth to inherit [?].
For the earth is everyone's home.
Since we entered this world weeping, we will also leave weeping. We came groaning, and we will also leave groaning.
For from the very first moment a person is born into the world, he weeps.
And again, when he is leaving the body, he weeps. We were born into suffering, and we will also depart into suffering.
For there is nothing lasting in human life except misery and sorrow.
Have you not heard what is written?
Do not let your hearts become weighed down with overeating, drunkenness, and the worries of life, so that that day comes upon you like a trap.
For it is coming upon everyone who lives on the face of the whole earth, whether king or ruler, rich or poor. Not a single person will escape that terrifying ordeal.
Do you not hear what is written: “Wealth will not benefit us on the day of wrath”?
Righteousness rescues a person from death.
But do not put your confidence in your money or in the prestige of wealth.
Do not make your soul secure through office and authority.
Afterward, gold or silver—all these things are dreams.
For wealth will not remain here, but our sins will go ahead of us and stand before God's judgment seat.
Have you yourself not heard what the Lord said: “Keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour”?
Let us therefore keep watch day and night, because we are not masters of our own bodies for even a single hour.
And we do not know when they will come looking for us.
Let us not make ourselves secure on the illusions of wealth. You do not know when they will call for you.
Have you not heard what is written: “No person can ransom another; no brother can ransom a brother”?
He cannot give God his ransom or the price for redeeming his soul.
It explains this as follows: no righteous father can ransom a sinful son, nor can a rich brother ransom a poor brother.
Nor can a righteous son ransom a sinful father. Rather, each person will receive according to what he has done.
Now then, my beloved, send your wealth ahead of you through acts of mercy toward the poor, so that you may find enjoyment without end.
Do not put your trust in the wealth of this world.
Do not make yourself secure on gold and silver.
Have you not heard Solomon
saying, “I hated all my wealth for which I had labored under the sun, because I must leave it to the person who comes after me”?
That is to say: a foolish person can scarcely say to himself, “I am gathering things for my children, so that they may find their livelihood after my death.”
How do you know, you fool, that your son will live and inherit from you, or that he will acquire great wealth and distribute it?
Will God not take care of your children without you?
Will God, who fed you, not also feed your children?
Was a single obol born along with you on the day you were born?
Now God has granted you this great wealth so that you may find rest both here and in the other place. But Satan has closed your heart.
He has not let you be compassionate toward the poor. Because of this, you will receive great, unending punishments for your unbelief.
For we have indeed seen many rich people accumulating money through great toil and business dealings, building themselves large houses and acquiring properties and extensive estates,
and gardens and fields, and many livestock, and a great deal of household goods, and large sums of money, saying, “We are saving up for our children.”
Yet even while they were thinking these things, their children were snatched away from them while still young.
Strangers seized the fruits of their toil. And they themselves, in turn,
went naked to God's judgment seat, with no good deed before them and no gift in their hands.
They cursed the day on which they were born into the world.
Do not say in your hardness of heart, “When I leave the body,
I will write my will, and my children and relatives will give alms for my soul.”
You senseless and utterly foolish person! Do you not know that when you leave the body, you will not own a single obol, nor will anyone remember you again?
You have money that you have accumulated.
You have a full storehouse.
You have vineyards.
You have houses that you built, but you have become a stranger to them.
They have ceased to be yours.
They have become the property of others.
If they wish, they give on your behalf; if they do not wish, they do not give on your behalf.
Have you not heard holy Job
saying, “I came out of my mother's womb naked, and I will depart again naked”?
The apostle also cries out, saying, “We brought nothing with us into this world, and we will take nothing when we leave.”
David also says, “Their spirit leaves them, and they return to their earth.”
You miserable person, what kind of person are you? What are these anxieties and these cares?
For you know the place of your birth, but you do not know the place of your death.
You know how many years you have lived until now, but you do not know how many more you will live.
Do you know how your parents, who brought you into the world, died?
Now then, my fellow human being, accept my advice. Let my counsel please you, and redeem your sins through acts of charity,
and your wrongdoings through compassion toward the poor, so that you may enjoy endless wealth.
Send gifts ahead of you before you leave the body, so that you may meet Christ with joy.
For someone who is going to meet a king of this world and find favor with him
sends gifts ahead of himself so that the king will welcome him.
How much more ought we to send acts of charity ahead of us to the King of all, who is surrounded by fear and trembling!
Solomon says, “Have all your provisions ready at hand.”
Give to charity according to your ability.
Do not say, “I have nothing to give.”
Remember the poor widow who put two small coins into the treasury.
Christ honored her because she gave everything she had to live on.
He also said, “Whoever gives one of these little ones even a single cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple—truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward.”
So do not neglect your salvation, my fellow human being, because of the material things of this life. We will not be left here forever.
Rather, a day will come when we leave it and become as though we had never entered it.
Remember the time when the sickness of death will come upon you, and you will lie down on your bed of your own accord and say, “I am sick today.”
After a while, the sickness will grow worse, and a high fever will seize your miserable flesh, together with great distress and pain.
Your bodily condition will become disturbed, your tongue will grow weak in your throat, and your speech will diminish in your mouth.
Your throat will become rigid, and no food will pass into it. The light of your eyes will gradually fail, and sweat will spread over your forehead.
Great bitterness will fill your heart. Your eyes will lose their skill, rolling and becoming troubled as the light gradually leaves them.
You will ask those who visit you, “What time is it?” because your senses have ceased to function within you.
Darkness and gloom have covered your eyes.
Your face has changed and become pale.
The hair has come loose.
The sinews of your hands and feet have stiffened.
Your heart and your soul have grown weaker, little by little.
You signal with your eyes, looking out for the terrifying powers that have come for you, hurrying to take you to the one who created you.
And when you see them, you open your mouth and give your spirit into the hands of the one who has come for you.
Oh, this great wonder and this great distress, more exhausting than any distress on earth!
Oh, the affliction that surpasses every affliction—the fear of death!
Then they take the soul and make it stand before God's terrifying judgment seat, to receive according to what it has done, whether good or evil.
O wise apostle Paul, your words are so very sweet!
For every person whom God has created, from Adam, the first human being, down to the one born today—when they leave the body,
they take their souls and make them stand before God's judgment seat, from the one who is a month old to the one who is a year old.
They bow down before the true Judge, and he pronounces sentence on them before they are taken to the places they deserve.
And again, on the day of the resurrection, their bodies will rise, free from decay,
and everyone's soul will return to their body once more, and they will receive according to what they have done, whether good or evil.
And we will be called to account for everything we have done in this place of exile, down to a little joking remark.
We will also be questioned about the thoughts of our hearts, just as our teacher and maker, Christ, said:
"Do not let any idle words come out of your mouths, for you will give an account of them on the day of judgment."
Blessed are those who will rise to a resurrection of life, for they will reign with Christ!
Woe to those who will be condemned to the second death because of their evil deeds!
But when the true Judge rises from the judgment seat, whoever has borne fruit has borne fruit.
But the chaff will be burned in a fire that cannot be put out.
The wheat, however, will be gathered into the storehouse, which is the kingdom of heaven.
Now, then, let us turn back and repent of our sins before they come looking for us.
Remember that it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
Tell me, then, what are all these schemes and all these troubles?
Are not three cubits of earth our home forever?
For whom are you storing things up?
From whom are you collecting interest?
For whom are you breaking the law?
Tell me, who will send these things down to you in the underworld?
Remember that you are not your own master for even a single day, but you spend your days on this earth like a hired laborer.
Whether you eat or drink, whether you fast, go hungry, or go thirsty, the sun sets every day, and every day your lifespan is shortened.
And when the number of your days is complete, they will not give you even a single hour's reprieve.
A human being is absolutely nothing.
A person today is earth and ashes tomorrow.
The person who eats and drinks today will have his mouth shut tomorrow.
The person who is eating at this very moment, who bathes in the baths and anoints himself with choice perfumes today, will tomorrow be bundled up in the tombs.
Stench has become his perfume.
The person who sleeps on couches, covered with fine linen, will tomorrow be thrown out among the tombs with the wild animals.
They have turned their backs on him.
They have left him in misery.
You miserable person! Eating and drinking could not save you today. Why did the possessions of your wealth not rescue you and give you a little care?
Why did the splendors of wealth not rescue you from these great afflictions?
Have you not heard about that rich man who was foolish like you, who said to his soul:
"You have many good things stored up for many years. Rest, eat, drink, and enjoy yourself"—thinking that he would spend a long time on earth.
Immediately God's sentence overtook him: "Fool! They will take your soul this very night. Who will own the things you have prepared?"
This is how it is with everyone who stores things up but is not rich in God.
Why, then, you fool, were your full storehouses unable to save you today?
Why were your clothes of pure silk and fine linen unable to rescue you today?
Why were the possessions you amassed in abundance unable to prevent God's sentence from overtaking you: "They will take your soul this very night"?
Have you not heard David say, "They will leave their wealth to others, and their tombs are their homes forever"?
The wise Solomon says, "Keep all your preparation at hand, for there is neither knowledge nor thought in the underworld, the place where you are going." That is:
When you leave this world, you will not be able to put anything right. Rather, the things you take with you when you go are the things by which and for which you will be judged.
Tell me, then, you fool, what are all these intrigues and these sins? You add sin to sin, lawlessness to lawlessness, deceit to deceit, and quarrel to quarrel.
Have you not remembered what is written: "Judgment is without mercy for the person who has not practiced [?]"? Remember that a person is like a shadow, and his days pass quickly.
A person's entire lifespan is like steam from a pot: it appears for a little while, then vanishes—especially in the case of a sinful person.
There is no gain in the life of evildoers, nor will he find any in the place where he is going. Instead, he will go from one suffering to another.
Even if he is a rich sinner, there is no rest in his life.
Have you not heard Solomon say, “He came in emptiness, and he will leave in emptiness. He came in sorrow, and he will leave in sorrow”?
As it is written, “There is no joy for the ungodly, says the Lord,” and again, “The hope of the ungodly will perish.”
And again, “The ungodly person is like chaff that the wind blows off the face of the earth.”
Tell me, then, sinner: what joy have you experienced throughout your entire life?
If you say, “I have spent my entire life being rich and enjoying myself thoroughly,” I will say to you plainly:
“What joy have you experienced throughout all your time living in sin?
Even if you are rich in gold and silver, what have you gained from being born on earth?”
This man, indeed, eats and drinks today.
Tomorrow, however, he is taken away from his wealth, and his mouth is shut so that he can eat no more from that moment on.
Tell me, sinful person: what rest do you have, since you are preoccupied all your life, collecting interest and doing business,
worrying day and night like someone who lacks bread,
with no comfort anywhere around you? Instead, your whole life is sorrow.
You build houses, country estates, and granaries, and you plant vineyards and gardens
and watering places. You do business and sail the sea, always like those in the agony of death.
You oppress the poor.
You bring accusations against strangers.
You plunder the houses of widows, preoccupied day and night,
although what you eat is bread, just like everyone else.
And while you are doing these things, the allotted span of your life comes to an end, and they wrap you up like a bundle of rags and carry you away.
The wealth you have accumulated will remain here, and the sins you have committed will go ahead of you to God's judgment seat.
And the houses you built will be images exposing your foolishness: others will live in them.
But your soul will be taken into the outer darkness because of your lawless deeds.
Others harvest the vineyards you planted, while you yourself long for a drop of water to moisten your tongue in Hades, like your brother Nineveh.
Tell me now, you merciless and sinful person: what have you gained from being born into the world?
Whether in your life or in your death, what have you gained except punishments that you have piled up for yourself because of your sins?
During your life you are distracted day and night,
wearing yourself out to increase your wealth. Then, at your death, you have gone to endless punishments as repayment for your lawless deeds.
But if the sinner is poor, you will find him working night and day because of the deprivation of his poverty,
while his children are hungry and naked, his wife is in need and worn down by hardship, and they curse one another.
There is no peace among them.
They are distracted day and night, living in distress with their children.
He often longs for death because of the suffering he is enduring.
Seeing his poverty, his wife's suffering, and his children's misery, he sins still more, committing thefts and swearing false oaths, as it is written: “Poverty humbles a person.”
And not only does it humble him, but it makes him practice deception and do things that God hates, as he wants to steal something to bring home for his wife and children.
And so he never stops being distracted by these worries throughout his entire life,
adding sin to sin as he spends his life, until his allotted lifespan is complete and he is suddenly taken away,
loaded down with the burden of his sins. He departs from poverty into endless poverty and great suffering.
Tell me now: what has this man gained from being born into the world, apart from suffering, misery, and heartache?
This is the one about whom it was written: “He came in futility, and he will go in futility, and his name will be covered in darkness.” But whether rich or poor,
woe to them for having been born into the world, because their visit to the world has turned out to their harm.
What comfort will there be for the person who dies in his sins, other than suffering and heartache in this place and the next?
Have you not heard what is written in Isaiah the prophet: “The sinner will reach a hundred years of age and be cursed”?
But tell me: have you ever enjoyed yourself, you sinful person?
Did you enjoy yourself when you were in your mother's womb?
How could you enjoy yourself, confined in darkness and its stench, knowing neither day nor night?
Did you enjoy yourself when you came out of your mother's womb?
How could you enjoy yourself?
For from the moment you were born, you were weeping and crying out.
For if you were comfortable, you would not weep. Weeping belongs to suffering.
Were you happy when you were being nursed at your mother's breasts?
How could you be happy?
You were crying all the time, with no understanding in you.
Were you happy when you were little?
How could you be happy?
Your face was always bent down toward the ground as you crawled on your hands and feet.
Your mouth was dribbling saliva, and if an animal trampled on you and killed you, you would not realize it.
Were you happy when your legs grew strong and you began to walk?
How could you be happy?
Your parents were disciplining you and sending you to a teacher so that you could learn a trade and make a living from it.
Were you happy when you grew up and reached maturity?
How could you be happy?
The youthful passions within you were fighting against you and would not leave you in peace for even a single hour.
Were you happy when you married?
No, you were not happy. Instead, you added even greater anxiety to your burdens.
Were you happy when you had children?
How could you be happy?
You were worrying about them [?] day and night.
For a man who has married and had children does not have a single hour of rest. Instead, worries weigh on him all the time. Especially if he is poor, his sufferings multiply upon him.
Were you happy when you grew old?
How could you be happy?
Your bones have broken down, the light of your eyes has faded, and your molars have fallen out and stopped chewing food. Your mind has stopped perceiving,
understanding a wise saying. The sinews of the body have loosened and can no longer rise with ease.
The mouth has withered and stopped speaking properly. The voice has grown weak. The ears have stopped hearing.
All these things have come upon you in your old age, especially another great sorrow: you have drawn near the grave, and you do not know how long they will ask after you.
Did you rejoice when your allotted time came to an end, because you were going to stand before God?
How will you rejoice at that time?
You lie on the bed of your suffering.
Intense heat surrounds you, and a severe illness weighs upon you. You groan over your sins because you have no good deeds before you.
You grieve over your little children, who will become orphans.
You are troubled by the distress that is upon you.
You look at the powers with shifting faces that have come for you.
You groan over the end of your life, because it has come so suddenly.
Did you rejoice, O man, as you stood before God's judgment seat?
How will you rejoice when you are weighed down by the burden of your sins?
You have no good deeds before you.
The angels of punishment seize your soul, their eyes shooting out flames of fire.
They roar at you and gnash their teeth at you.
Your sins follow you, acting as your accusers.
Where will you turn your face, you wretched one? Or where will you look for relief, when there is neither right nor left?
Here are the poor whom you oppressed.
Here are the needy and the strangers whom you defrauded.
You consumed what belonged to them.
Here are the false oaths.
Here are the slanders.
Look at the hatred.
Here are the acts of envy.
Here are the quarrels.
Here are the defilements.
Here are the defilements.
Here are the acts of sexual immorality.
Here are the murders and all the other evil deeds you have committed.
Then, at that moment, the judge cries out, “Throw him into the outer darkness! There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there.”
This is the end of every sinner who has not repented of their sins before dying.
Look, I have made the matter clear to you: there is no benefit in a person's life, in being born into this world.
If you want to be saved and inherit life, hurry and redeem your sins through acts of mercy
and compassion toward the poor, so that you may enjoy yourself in the place where there is joy and rejoicing.
And even if you have committed every sin, turn back and repent. God will forgive you.
For he is merciful and loves humanity. He relents over the evils of those who turn to him.
He says, “I do not desire the sinner's death, but rather that he turn away from his evil way, repent, and live.”

And again, “If the lawless person turns away from his wicked deeds and does what is right, I will not remember the lawless acts he committed. Instead, he will live by the righteousness he has practiced.”
He says, “Return to me, children who have strayed, and I will heal your brokenness.”
He says with his mouth, which is full of life, “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”
And again, “Come to me, all who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.”
Do you see God's love for humanity toward us, O human being?
So do not keep putting things off, day after day, month after month, year after year, until the allotted time of your life comes to an end
and you depart weighed down by the load of your sins, and curse the day on which you were born.
I have said all these things to you, my beloved, because of the written saying, “A human being is born for suffering.”
For the prophet considered that there is no benefit in human life apart from suffering and misery.
That is why he said, “A human being is born for suffering, and his days pass quickly.”
But as for the righteous, their whole life is joy and gladness, because they were born for blessing, and they will also go to perfect blessing.
Truly, the righteous person is fortunate and blessed to have been born into the world.
This is truly the person whose course in the world has proved beneficial to him.
Blessed is the righteous and merciful person, for he will eat the good things of the earth and rest in the kingdom of heaven beside the patriarchs.
Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Job, these faithful men.
And blessed is the poor person who is grateful, cheerful, and wise, for he will leave the poverty of this world and be brought into endless wealth.
This is truly the person whose sufferings have ended and who has inherited the rest that will never end.
As it is written, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”
And again, “Blessed is the person whom you will receive to yourself, Lord.” And again, “One day in your courts is better than a thousand outside them.”
Now, my beloved, we have said these things to you about the consolation of the soul.
I have drawn out my speech a little.
I know that the tears that have flowed from your eyes will become a spring of salvation for you,
and it will cleanse your bodies at the great feast of the commander, Saint Victor, whose feast we are celebrating today.
Believe me, you people who love God: I did not want to bring up this subject, so full of sorrow, at this great feast today,
lest I cast a shadow over the feast of Saint Victor, who is honored among all the martyrs. But I was compelled in my thoughts.
It was as though I saw the commander standing before me,
stirring up joy in my heart and mind through his love for us, saying to me, “Speak, man, to these people for the salvation of their souls.
Bring them into the harbor of salvation on the day of my commemoration, so that they repent of their sins. This is a greater tribute to me than ten thousand speeches of praise.
For I do not want honor that belongs to this world, since my honor is in heaven, beside my Lord, my King, Christ.”
When I heard these things from Saint Victor, who cares for all who suffer,
since he had declined his own honor for the sake of the salvation and restoration of our soul and body,
I then turned my tongue toward you, my sons and daughters.
I said these few things to you about the consolation of our soul.
Now, then, let us send ahead of us the things we will find for our soul on the day of our need,
so that Saint Victor, whose feast we celebrate today, will intercede for us before Christ, the true shepherd,
and lead our souls into the pastures that please him, as it is written: “His wishes are more precious than gold and an abundance of precious stones.”
Let us pay attention to what we hear, lest we drift away, according to the words of the wise Paul.
Let us turn away from our sins before we are sought out.
You have sinned, O man, in your foolishness. Turn back and repent, and God will forgive you.
And again, if you have not sinned, watch yourself so that the devil does not envy you.
For he is cunning and hates the human race. Listen to what is written in the general letters: “Be sober and keep watch,
because your adversary, the devil, goes about roaring like lions, looking to devour [?] souls.”
Paul also says, “Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the rulers and the authorities,
against the world-rulers of darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavens.”
Our Savior also commands us, saying, “If the owner of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would have kept watch and would not have allowed his house to be broken into.
So keep watch yourselves, because you do not know at what time the thief is coming.”
You understand, then, my dear friends, that a person must watch over himself day and night, so that the devil does not envy him and destroy his righteousness.
Do not despair and say, “I have committed many sins. God will not forgive me if I repent.”
Watch yourself; do not speak like that.
Do not give sin power over you.
Even if you have committed a multitude of sins, turn back and repent, and God will forgive you and count you among those who have never sinned at all.
For it is like grapes: when they emerge from the vine, you find them sour.
But when the vine is tended and water is put around its roots, the grapes that were sour before, after a little while—
their sourness will disappear, so that you cannot tell where their sourness has gone, and they become sweet to the taste.
This is how sin is wiped away through repentance, and righteousness springs up sweetly in the people who practice it.
You have seen, my dear friends, how Saint Victor has gladdened us at today's great festival by setting a spiritual table before us.
Truly, this holy speech of praise is medicine for us.
The meaning of the holy Scriptures is entirely comforting.
This eulogy is a healer for everyone.
For it saves those who stand and raises those who have fallen.
Let us, in turn, observe what we hear, and we will be saved.
Let us not become careless and continue sinning, lest we be taken away suddenly and depart in shame and sorrow. But I have almost entered another arena.
I have forgotten the mighty deeds and wonders of Saint Victor, whose festival we are celebrating today.
Our excessive negligence has brought us down into this great sorrow, so that we have forgotten the honored commander.
For my tongue is very weak, and I cannot speak of even one ten-thousandth of your virtues.
But like a person who is about to approach a great sea or a great spring.
Then you find him drawing water and dipping into the spring as it gushes up ever more abundantly. Such is my own situation before that man's achievements.
For I began to speak about his mighty deeds and the wonders he performed at the beginning of this speech in his praise.
Then they carried me away in my mind and thoughts, prompting me to speak with you about the salvation of [?] souls at his great feast.
We know that Saint Victor rejoices over the words of admonition that we speak into the ears of the disciples in this speech in his praise.
But when he saw most of the people distressed at heart and weeping over the words of admonition that we were speaking—
I was afraid that I might bring sorrow upon the people at today's great feast.
I turned the rudder of my tongue to tell you about a few miracles that took place at his shrine, which I saw with my own eyes, to the glory of God, who honors those who honor him.
I do indeed wish to recount a few of his achievements, but I am at a loss, because my tongue cannot honor him as he deserves.
For our God-bearing fathers, the bishops who came before me, namely Eusebius, Julius, and Innocent—
these true teachers who bear God—some of them undertook to speak of your honor and the wonders you perform at your shrine.
Yet they could not fully recount your virtues and your miraculous signs.
How much less can I, this poor, despised, uneducated man!
How will I be able to draw water from the sea of your achievements? That is why I have placed my finger over my mouth,
knowing that I cannot describe your gift.
In particular, through your holy intercessions you have eased the illness that spreads over my feet from time to time.
For great is the grace that God has given you.
He has established these signs of healing permanently at your shrine: the mute speak, the lame walk, and lepers are cleansed.
You cast out demons and raise the dead through the great gift that God has established permanently in your shrines.
It was not only in the place where your body lies that signs of this kind continued to occur, but in every place throughout the whole world
over which your name is invoked, these signs continue to occur in them all. So that you may know that what I am telling you is true,
listen, and I will tell you this great wonder, to the glory of God and Saint Victor.
There was a man in this city who possessed great wealth, many properties, country estates, and vineyards.
He was a very good man who loved the poor, and he had great faith in Saint Victor.

Consequently, every year he would give large quantities of wine to the shrine, for them to use in celebrating the services and to distribute to the sick and those in need, for the salvation of his soul.
And his offering was continually present at the saint’s shrine throughout his lifetime.
But the good God, through the intercessions of Saint Victor,
blessed the man.
made him rich.
And he prospered greatly.
God’s blessing abounded in his household, his gardens, his vineyards, and his fields, and his crops increased greatly, so that the blessing the Lord had allotted him was beyond measure.
The man increased the charitable meals and offerings that he gave to God in the name of Saint Victor.
His possessions increased greatly, his crops were exceptionally fine, and his livestock were beyond counting.
He never stopped observing these practices, even into his old age.
Finally, he fell ill with the sickness from which he would die.
He called his son and said to him, “My son, look, I am about to go the way of all the earth.
Be diligent in showing mercy to the poor and everyone in need, just as you see me doing. Above all, the offering to my lord Saint Victor:
do not neglect it, but increase it, because he is the one who blessed us and granted us this great wealth and these many possessions.
And let your acts of mercy and your charitable meals increase, so that they may open the gates of the kingdom of heaven for you.”
His son answered, “I will do everything you tell me.” And so the man let go and died.
They laid him beside his ancestors.
His son took possession of his wealth and his property.
But his heart was not wholly devoted to God like his father’s, as was written about Solomon. Instead, he was merciless toward the poor.
From then on, he disregarded his father’s will,
and he did not observe the things his father had told him.
He became negligent about the charitable meals and the offering that his father used to provide.
He ate and drank indulgently.
He cast aside the fear of God and his father’s instructions.
When the grape-harvest season arrived, the steward of Saint Victor’s shrine sent the clerics to him to collect the firstfruits, according to his father’s custom.
But he would not give them anything. Instead, he said maliciously, “My father certainly hated his own property! Does Saint Victor drink wine? No, it is the clerics who drink it!
Still, whenever they gather [?].”
Am I to send the offering and the firstfruits so that they can hold services? No! I will not give this much wine. Instead, I will keep it and use it to pay the taxes and my hired worker.”
So in his foolishness he withheld the saint’s offering.
He did not remember what is written: “Love does not seek its own interests.”
Then he harvested the vineyards on the estates, as his father had customarily done.
He found an immeasurable quantity of wine.

He brought it into the storehouses, saying, “I will keep it until the time when the merchants from Palestine come, as they used to come to my father every year. Then I will sell it and receive large sums of money for it.”
What, then, would Saint Victor do, since his offering had been treated with contempt because of the love of money?
In an instant he made the wine, which had been excellent a little earlier, turn into vinegar saturated with salt.
His possessions also began to slip from his hands. Yet he did not realize that God’s hand was upon him because of his contempt.
One day the merchants came and brought him a great deal of gold to buy his wine.
They found it completely spoiled.
It had turned sour and become infested with worms.
They were utterly astonished.
Afterward they opened the door of another storehouse.
Again, they found them even worse than these.
In short, they examined all the wine.
They found it unusable.
They said to him, “Truly, we are astonished at this wine. What has happened to it since your father passed away?
Perhaps you have neglected it. Otherwise, we do not know what has happened to it.”
So the merchants took the gold back from him.
They returned to their homeland.
He was left deeply distressed and grieving.
After some days he became aware of the sin he had committed: it was Saint Victor who had ruined his produce, because he had treated his holy offering with contempt.
He kept saying, “Woe to me! I did not obey my father’s instruction. Instead, greed blinded my eyes.
I wanted to take the martyr’s offering away from him.
Look! He has ruined all my produce.
I do not know what I will do from now on.”
That night Saint Victor came to the man in great, indescribable glory.
And he said to him with a stern warning, “Since greed has blinded your eyes,
you have seized the offering that your father gives to God in my name.
Look, I in turn have struck all your crops.
I have turned them into thorns and stubble.
And I will strike your grapevines so that they bear no fruit, because of your insolence.
As for you yourself, I came to bring great suffering upon you and strike you dead, but I remembered your father’s righteousness.
Nevertheless, since you have treated the offering for my sanctuary with contempt,
I in turn will cause all your wine to spoil.”
The man was terrified and said, “My lord, who are you, with such great glory surrounding you?”
He answered, “I am Victor the general.
I am the one who blessed your father’s property.
I made him prosper in wheat and wine.
I doubled his wealth, his livestock, and all his possessions for him, because of his acts of mercy toward the poor and the offerings he gives to God in my name.
But since you did not obey your father or remember the fear of God, but instead eagerly stole the offering for my martyr’s shrine,
I in turn have repaid you.
I have destroyed the fruit of your labor.
